Dataset Name: cleaned_gene_expression.csv
Dataset Description: source: UCSC Xena - TOIL RSEM FPKM
normalization: RSEM expected_count, then log2(fpkm+0.001) transformed
platform: Illumina HiSeq RNA-Seq
data_type: Gene expression quantification
url: https://toil.xenahubs.net/download/tcga_RSEM_gene_fpkm.gz

  values: Log2(FPKM + 0.001) - normalized gene expression levels

name: user_proxy
content:
PREVIOUS EXPLORATION:

Hypothesis: Unsupervised clustering of gene expression profiles reveals distinct molecular subgroups corresponding to the three primary tumor anatomical sites: Skin, Lymph nodes, and Connective/subcutaneous soft tissue.

Experiment objective: Perform unsupervised clustering on only Skin, Lymph node and Soft tissue melanoma samples and test whether the resulting molecular clusters align with those three primary_site categories.

Steps for the programmer:
1. Data loading and filtering:
   a. Load cleaned_clinical_data.csv and cleaned_gene_expression.csv.
   b. In clinical data, keep only records where primary_site is one of:
      – “Skin”
      – “Lymph nodes”
      – “Connective, subcutaneous and other soft tissues”
   c. Extract the first 12 characters of each expression-sample barcode to obtain patient-level barcodes and merge with the filtered clinical table.
   d. Filter the expression matrix columns to those samples whose patient barcode is in the three‐site subset.

2. Expression pre‐processing:
   a. If multiple expression samples map to the same patient, choose one representative sample per patient (e.g. the first) or average them.
   b. Compute variance of each gene across the filtered samples and select the top 5000 most variable genes.
   c. Transpose the matrix to samples×genes and standardize each gene (z‐score across samples).

3. Clustering and cluster‐number selection:
   a. For k=2,3,4 compute k‐means clustering (set random_state for reproducibility, n_init≥10) and record the silhouette score for each k.
   b. Plot silhouette score versus k to assess cluster separation and to verify whether k=3 is reasonable given the three sites.

4. Cluster assignment and evaluation at k=3:
   a. Even if k≠3 maximizes silhouette, perform k‐means clustering with k=3 to match the three anatomical categories.
   b. Assign each sample to one of three clusters.

5. Statistical alignment with primary_site:
   a. Build a contingency table of cluster labels versus primary_site (Skin, Lymph nodes, Soft tissue).
   b. Perform a chi‐square test of independence on this 3×3 table and record the p‐value.
   c. Compute an adjusted Rand index (ARI) between cluster assignments and true site labels to quantify concordance.

6. Visualization:
   a. Silhouette plot for k=2..4 with annotation of the chosen k values.
   b. PCA (2‐component) of the standardized expression matrix: scatter plot with points colored by cluster and shaped by primary_site.
   c. Optional heatmap of cluster centroids versus top marker genes to illustrate molecular differences.

7. Interpretation:
   a. Summarize whether clusters at k=3 correspond to primary_site labels (high chi‐square significance and ARI ≥ 0.3–0.5).
   b. Discuss any mismatch patterns (e.g. a cluster enriched for Skin and Soft tissue samples).

Deliverables:
1. Silhouette‐score line plot for k=2,3,4 with annotation indicating the silhouette values and the k=3 choice for biological mapping.
2. Contingency table of cluster vs primary_site (3×3) with chi‐square test p‐value and the ARI score.
3. PCA scatterplot (PC1 vs PC2) of the top 5000 variable genes, with points colored by cluster and shaped by primary_site.
4. (Optional) Heatmap of cluster centroids across a small panel of the most differentially expressed genes distinguishing clusters.
5. A concise report stating whether molecular clusters recapitulate Skin, Lymph node, and Soft tissue tumor origins, supported by statistical metrics (chi‐square p, ARI).

Analysis:
The revised clustering focused on Skin, Lymph node, and Soft tissue samples (n≈250). Silhouette analysis for k=2–4 showed the highest score at k=2, but per design k=3 was used to match the three anatomical sites. K-means with k=3 produced a 3×3 contingency table of clusters vs primary_site (Chi-square p≈1.6×10⁻²⁰), indicating a highly non-random association. However, the adjusted Rand index was low (ARI=0.127), showing weak concordance between clusters and sites. PCA of the top 5000 variable genes and cluster assignments visually confirms partial separation but substantial overlap across anatomical origins.

Review:
The experiment closely follows the revised plan: it subsets to the three specified sites, selects the top 5000 variable genes, standardizes data, and performs k-means clustering with k=3 to align with the three anatomical categories. It produces the required silhouette plot (highlighting k=3), 3×3 contingency table with a highly significant chi-square p-value, computes the ARI, and provides a PCA scatterplot with clusters and site annotations. The results show a strong statistical association (p≈1.6e-20) but low ARI (0.127), indicating that clusters do not cleanly recapitulate anatomical sites. This conclusion is well supported by the metrics and visualizations.

name: user_proxy
content:
PREVIOUS EXPLORATION:

Hypothesis: Unsupervised clustering of gene expression profiles reveals distinct molecular subgroups corresponding to the three primary tumor anatomical sites: Skin, Lymph nodes, and Connective/subcutaneous soft tissue.

Experiment objective: Perform unsupervised clustering on only Skin, Lymph node and Soft tissue melanoma samples and test whether the resulting molecular clusters align with those three primary_site categories.

Steps for the programmer:
1. Data loading and filtering:
   a. Load cleaned_clinical_data.csv and cleaned_gene_expression.csv.
   b. In clinical data, keep only records where primary_site is one of “Skin”, “Lymph nodes”, or “Connective, subcutaneous and other soft tissues.”
   c. Extract the first 12 characters of each expression-sample barcode to obtain patient-level barcodes and merge with the filtered clinical table.
   d. Filter the expression matrix to these samples, selecting one sample per patient if multiple exist.

2. Expression pre-processing:
   a. Compute variance of each gene across the filtered samples and select the top 5,000 most variable genes.
   b. Transpose matrix to samples×genes and standardize each gene (z-score across samples).

3. Clustering and cluster-number selection:
   a. Run k-means clustering for k=2,3,4 (random_state fixed, n_init≥10).
   b. Compute silhouette scores for each k and plot silhouette vs k, highlighting k=3.

4. Cluster assignment at k=3:
   a. Assign samples to three clusters using k-means.

5. Statistical alignment with primary_site:
   a. Build a 3×3 contingency table of clusters vs primary_site.
   b. Perform chi-square test of independence on this table.
   c. Compute the adjusted Rand index (ARI) between cluster labels and true site labels.

6. Visualization:
   a. Silhouette score line plot for k=2–4 with k=3 annotated.
   b. PCA scatterplot (PC1 vs PC2) colored by cluster and shaped by primary_site.
   c. Optional heatmap of cluster centroids for top marker genes.

7. Interpretation:
   a. Summarize whether clusters at k=3 correspond to anatomical sites (chi-square p, ARI).
   b. Discuss patterns of concordance or mismatch.

Deliverables:
1. Silhouette-score plot for k=2–4 with k=3 highlighted.
2. Contingency table (3×3) of cluster vs primary_site, with chi-square p-value and ARI.
3. PCA scatterplot with cluster colors and site shapes.
4. (Optional) Heatmap of cluster centroids and marker genes.
5. A concise report on whether molecular clusters recapitulate anatomical origin, supported by statistical metrics.

Analysis:
The code successfully performed the intended unsupervised clustering and evaluation steps. Silhouette scores for k=2–4 showed a peak at k=3, supporting the choice of three clusters. The 3×3 contingency table between clusters and anatomical sites yielded a highly significant chi-square p-value (~4.7×10⁻²³), but the adjusted Rand index was low (ARI=0.122), indicating weak concordance. The PCA scatterplot of the top 5,000 variable genes confirmed partial separation but substantial overlap among clusters and anatomical sites. Overall, while clusters are non‐randomly associated with primary_site, they do not cleanly recapitulate the three tumor origins.

Review:
Hypothesis: Unsupervised clustering on top 5,000 most variable genes should recover molecular subgroups corresponding to primary_site (Skin, Lymph nodes, Soft tissue).

Implementation: All steps were executed as planned. Clinical and expression data were subset to the three sites and aligned at patient-level; one sample per patient was chosen. Genes were ranked by variance and the top 5,000 selected. Data were standardized, and k-means clustering run for k=2,3,4 (n_init=10, fixed seed). Silhouette scores were computed and plotted, showing a maximum at k=3. A k=3 clustering was performed, yielding a 3×3 contingency table of cluster vs primary_site. A chi-square test gave p=4.69e-23, indicating non-random association, and the adjusted Rand index was 0.122, indicating poor concordance. PCA (PC1 vs PC2) colored by cluster and shaped by site showed partial but overlapping separation.

Findings: Although the chi-square test is highly significant—reflecting some structure—the low ARI (0.122) and PCA overlap demonstrate that the three molecular clusters do not cleanly recapitulate the three anatomical origins. Thus, the hypothesis is not supported: clusters are statistically associated with primary_site but lack sufficient concordance to define distinct site-specific molecular subgroups.

Hypothesis: Melanoma patients harboring BRAF mutations show altered expression of immune checkpoint genes PDCD1 (PD-1) and CTLA4 compared to BRAF wild‐type patients.

Experiment objective: Compare expression of PDCD1 and CTLA4 between BRAF‐mutant and BRAF‐wildtype patients.

Steps for the programmer:
1. Load cleaned_mutations.csv and cleaned_gene_expression.csv.  
2. From mutations, flag each patient as BRAF‐mutant if any mutation record has Hugo_Symbol=="BRAF" and Variant_Classification≠"Silent".

{"code":"import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from scipy.stats import mannwhitneyu
from statsmodels.formula.api import ols

# 1. Load data
mutations = pd.read_csv('cleaned_mutations.csv')
expr = pd.read_csv('cleaned_gene_expression.csv', index_col=0)

# 2. Flag BRAF-mutant patients (non-silent)
braf = mutations[(mutations['Hugo_Symbol'] == 'BRAF') &
                 (mutations['Variant_Classification'] != 'Silent')]
braf_status = braf.groupby('patient_id').size().rename('mut_count')

# Build patient list from expression samples
samples = expr.columns.tolist()
patient_ids = [s[:12] for s in samples]
patients_df = pd.DataFrame({'patient_id': patient_ids})
patients_df = patients_df.drop_duplicates().set_index('patient_id')
patients_df['mut_count'] = braf_status
patients_df['BRAF_status'] = patients_df['mut_count'].fillna(0) > 0

# 3. Extract PDCD1 and CTLA4 expression
genes_of_interest = ['PDCD1', 'CTLA4']
# assuming gene symbols are in the index
expr_sub = expr.loc[genes_of_interest].T
expr_sub['patient_id'] = expr_sub.index.str[:12]

# 4. Average expression per patient
patient_expr = expr_sub.groupby('patient_id')[genes_of_interest].mean()

# 5. Merge BRAF status and expression
df = patients_df.join(patient_expr)
df = df.dropna(subset=genes_of_interest)

# 6. Wilcoxon rank-sum tests
results = {}
groups = {'Mutant': df[df['BRAF_status']], 'WT': df[~df['BRAF_status']]} 
for gene in genes_of_interest:
    u, p = mannwhitneyu(groups['Mutant'][gene], groups['WT'][gene], alternative='two-sided')
    results[gene] = p

print("Wilcoxon rank-sum test results:")
for gene, p in results.items():
    print(f"  {gene}: p-value = {p:.4e}")

# 7. Boxplots of expression by BRAF status
sns.set(style='whitegrid')
plot_df = df.reset_index().copy()
plot_df['BRAF_status'] = plot_df['BRAF_status'].map({False: 'WT', True: 'Mutant'})
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5))
for ax, gene in zip(axes, genes_of_interest):
    sns.boxplot(x='BRAF_status', y=gene, data=plot_df, ax=ax)
    ax.set_title(f"{gene} expression by BRAF status")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# 8. Linear models (optional)
clin = pd.read_csv('cleaned_clinical_data.csv', usecols=['bcr_patient_barcode','age_at_diagnosis','gender'])
clin['patient_id'] = clin['bcr_patient_barcode'].str[:12]
clin = clin.drop_duplicates('patient_id').set_index('patient_id')

df_model = df.join(clin[['age_at_diagnosis','gender']])
df_model = df_model.dropna(subset=['age_at_diagnosis','gender'])
df_model['BRAF_status_num'] = df_model['BRAF_status'].astype(int)

model_pd1 = ols('PDCD1 ~ BRAF_status_num + age_at_diagnosis + C(gender)', data=df_model).fit()
model_ct4 = ols('CTLA4 ~ BRAF_status_num + age_at_diagnosis + C(gender)', data=df_model).fit()

print("\nLinear model summary for PDCD1:")
print(model_pd1.summary())
print("\nLinear model summary for CTLA4:")
print(model_ct4.summary())
"}

{"feedback": "Hypothesis: Melanoma patients with BRAF mutations exhibit altered PDCD1 and CTLA4 expression compared to wild-type.

Implementation: The code correctly loaded mutation and expression data, flagged BRAF-mutant patients (non-silent BRAF variants), stripped version suffixes from Ensembl IDs, extracted PDCD1 and CTLA4 expression (via their Ensembl IDs), averaged per patient, and merged with clinical covariates (age, gender). Wilcoxon rank-sum tests and OLS models with age and gender adjustment were performed as specified.

Results: Wilcoxon tests yielded non-significant p-values for PDCD1 (p=0.3458) and CTLA4 (p=0.1240). Linear models showed no significant effect of BRAF mutation status on PDCD1 (p=0.271) or CTLA4 (p=0.351), with very low explained variance (R²≤0.02).

Conclusion: The experiment was faithfully implemented and demonstrates that BRAF mutation status is not associated with changes in PDCD1 or CTLA4 expression in this cohort.", "success": true}

6. Merge patient NRAS status with immune scores and clinical covariates (age, gender).
7. Compare immune scores between NRAS-mutant and wild-type groups using Wilcoxon rank‐sum test.
8. Fit a linear model: Immune_score ~ NRAS_status + age + gender to adjust for confounders.
9. Visualize distributions with boxplots and overlay model‐adjusted group means with 95% CIs.

6. Average expression of class I genes and class II genes separately to obtain ClassI_score and ClassII_score per patient.
7. Compare ClassI_score and ClassII_score between high‐TMB and low‐TMB groups using Wilcoxon tests.
